hook.line: Tomás has just realised that cooking for a whole café is nothing like cooking for himself. In English you would say "cooking" and "waiting" as if they were nouns. Spanish does the same job with the plain infinitive.
hook.es: Cocinar para tanta gente no es fácil.
hook.en: Cooking for so many people isn't easy.

rule:
English turns a verb into a noun by adding *-ing*: "cooking is easy", "waiting bothers me". Spanish needs no change. The plain infinitive (*cocinar*, *esperar*) can stand at the start of the sentence like any noun.

*Cocinar es fácil.*
*Esperar me molesta.*

The verb that follows is always singular, even when the infinitive has a long tail: *Hablar español todos los días es útil*.

For "not doing", put *no* in front of the infinitive: *No saber la palabra me da pena*.

The infinitive also follows feeling verbs such as *me encanta*, *me molesta*, *me da pena*: *Me encanta caminar por el barrio*. There is never a Spanish *-ando* or *-iendo* in these spots.
smallPrint: Teachers call this the infinitive used as a noun, or a substantive infinitive. In careful writing you will also see *el* in front: *el saber*.

yourTurn.prompt: Choose the right form and type the whole sentence (Living in Bogotá is an adventure): *___ en Bogotá es una aventura.* (*Vivir* or *Viviendo*)
yourTurn.answer: Vivir en Bogotá es una aventura.
yourTurn.why: The subject of the sentence is a plain infinitive, never an *-ando* or *-iendo* form.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: Cooking is easy.
yourTurn.why: The infinitive does the job of "cooking", and the verb after it stays singular.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: Waiting bothers me.
yourTurn.why: *Esperar* is the subject, and *me molesta* says it bothers you.

yourTurn.prompt: Ask a friend if waiting bothers them.
yourTurn.why: *Te* is your friend, and *esperar* is the thing that bothers.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it negative (Cooking isn't easy): *Cocinar es fácil.*
yourTurn.why: *No* goes in front of *es*, as always.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: Not knowing the word embarrasses me.
yourTurn.answer: No saber la palabra me da pena.
yourTurn.why: *No* in front of the infinitive means "not doing".

yourTurn.prompt: Make it about *we* (We love walking around the neighbourhood): *Me encanta caminar por el barrio.*
yourTurn.answer: Nos encanta caminar por el barrio.
yourTurn.why: *Nos encanta* is "we love", and *caminar* stays as it is.

pitfalls.why: Almost. English "cooking" ends in *-ing*, but Spanish uses the plain infinitive as the subject.
After a feeling verb like *me molesta*, Spanish wants the infinitive, not an *-ando* form.
The subject is one action, so the verb is singular, whatever comes after it.
To say "not doing", put *no* in front of the infinitive.

personal: Say one true thing about yourself with an infinitive as the subject, for example *Me encanta cocinar* or *Esperar me molesta*.
